newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German tax talks to resume on March 8.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German tax talks to resume on March 8.

text.p: Germany's coalition and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) agreed on Friday to hold a third round of talks next week to try and agree a package of tax reforms to give jobs and investment a much-needed boost.

The two sides will meet again on Saturday, March 8, but came away from a meeting of a working group of six with widely diverging views on chances of a deal to battle record post-war unemployment of 4.7 million.
"Deep-seated differences remain," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told reporters after the talks. But, he added: "It still seems sensible to continue the talks."
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said his hopes had risen that a deal could be struck by the end of March.
"We look with great optimism to the chances of agreement in the further talks," Schaeuble told a separate briefing.
"The way is long and will require great efforts, but the chances of reaching an agreement enabling us to fight unemployment have increased."

Hermann Otto Solms of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) was also upbeat. "We are very happy that these talks are taking place, because they open the chances to agree and implement such reforms more quickly," he said.

Under discussion was a 30 billion marks ($17.7 billion) coalition package of tax cuts to be phased in over two years. It plans reductions in income and corporate taxes, but a proposed fall in top-rate income tax to 39 from 53 percent is disputed by the SPD.
An early deal could enable cuts to be phased in sooner, boosting the economy as Bonn tries to make the grade for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Failure, meanwhile, would condemn the measures to long wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can block tax changes through its majority in the upper house of parliament.

The two sides agree broadly on the need to cut corporation tax to 35 percent from 47. But Scharping said they remained far apart on top-rate income tax -- which he called a "secondary issue" -- and on the issue of labour overheads.
Separate to the tax reform, Scharping demanded that over half of the 57 billion marks in non-welfare items carried by occupational insurance schemes be removed by this July.
But Finance Minister Theo Waigel said that could not come without counter-financing from the budget.
"We can't just give good news. So wheover wants to announce the good news must also give the bad news that there would have also to be a rise in indirect taxes," he said.
Scharping, however, ruled out a rise in value-added tax to finance tax and benefit changes, as well as any moves to cut tax relief on pay for night, weekend and holiday work.

The two sides did manage to clear most of their differences in their calculations of the impact of the tax cuts. An initial gap of over 30 billion marks was cut to around six billion, and should be cleared on the basis of new statistical data.
Friday's tax talks followed a heated parliamentary clash between the coalition and SPD in a debate over abolishing a capital trading tax -- a row which has dragged for two years.
The Bundestag lower house passed the bill with a 330 to 293 majority, but the SPD said it would block the measure in the upper house. Waigel said the tax's abolition was long overdue.
"We could have abolished the capital trading tax long ago if you in the SPD had not prevented it, and then thousands of people could have been working today," he told the Bundestag.

The SPD said the government was playing fast and loose by planning to compensate local governments for lost revenue with a share of a turnover tax without making necessary changes to the constitution.
"You want the Bundestag to pass a law which is clearly unconstitutional," SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said. "Even if is constitutional, it violates legislative hygiene."

The capital trading tax is levied only in western Germany, and would have to be introduced automatically in the former communist east if it is not abolished. That, Waigel said, would damage the capital base of struggling companies there.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.691 German Marks)
